interludes.label: Morning Tea
interludes.title: Morning Tea
interludes.synopsis: Pixel brings tea handle-first. She knows his comings and goings without being asked. The half-step back almost fires — and doesn't.
interludes.text:
The Pivot's hallway at six in the morning: overhead strips on their pre-dawn setting, half-power, the kind of light that asked nothing back. The air at this hour had the West Town character — solder, old iron, the diesel rise from the freight tier three blocks south coming up through the vent gaps whenever the wind shifted east. Kyle had been breathing it for four years. He noticed it only when he was this awake this early, which was becoming a category he visited more than he preferred to count.

His door was 2W. Hers was 2E. He'd been in the hallway forty seconds when hers opened.

Pixel had two cups. She held one out handle-first, and he reached and took it before he'd committed to an opinion about what it meant.

The tea was green. Liang blend. Still too hot to drink with any dignity.

"The vending strip on two had it this week," she said. She was leaning against the doorframe, her own cup near her collarbone, not quite drinking. There was a fresh solder burn on her right forefinger — calibration slip, two days old at most — and she had the look of a woman who'd been awake longer than she was acknowledging. "Figured you'd want to taste it before you knew where it came from."

Kyle tasted it.

It was the right blend. He hadn't told her it was the right blend. That information existed in the pattern of what he bought on the weeks he had money for preferences, and she had been reading the pattern, and here it was in a cup already turned toward him.

"You came in at twenty past midnight on Tuesday," she said, in the same voice she used to read a calibration result back to him — precise, informational, not asking anything from him with it. "Wednesday closer to two. Last night was three-twelve."

He held the cup.

"The east hinge drags worse on the pull than the push," she said. "Different sound from when you're moving quiet on purpose." A pause. Short. "You weren't moving quiet."

The half-step back started.

The mechanism that had been running at standard function for four years — the small managed distance, the redirect, the posture that said nothing wrong here, I just don't do this — it registered the situation and it started. He felt it start. He felt the weight shift.

It did not take the step.

Kyle drank the tea. The too-hot kind that costs something at the back of the throat. His neuretics logged the damage gradient against some longer tally they kept for him, a quiet accounting running two levels below the morning. He didn't look at the number. He drank the rest of the cup.

"Three-twelve," he said.

"Give or take a minute."

She had shifted her attention to the far wall. The particular quality of the way she was not looking at him said she understood the weight in the hallway and had decided, somewhere around the time she was steeping the tea, not to do anything with it. Not because she hadn't seen it. Because she'd already accounted for it, the way she accounted for everything: the hinge drag, the exact hour, the blend he preferred.

Her knowing him had become her keeping track of him.

He didn't name that. Neither did she.

"The hinge," he said. "I'll sort it."

"Already oiled it." She pushed off the doorframe, easy as air pressure shifting. "Catches again by Thursday. No point until it does."

Her door swung shut behind her. Pull side, smooth and quiet, the oil still doing its work.

Kyle stood in the hallway with the empty cup. The overhead strips ran at their half-power. The linoleum was worn through at both their thresholds — two bare patches of concrete facing each other like the evidence of a habit neither of them had named. Three floors down, the freight tier was coming awake, the low rumble of it just below the register where the mind decided to assign attention.

He stood there a moment longer than was necessary.

Then he went back inside.

interludes.label: Eat Something
interludes.title: Eat Something
interludes.synopsis: Pixel brings food and holster advice before the corridor job. Kyle takes the food. He doesn't fix the holster. The corridor fight costs him.
interludes.text:
She knocked twice, a long gap, once. Kyle's pattern for the door, which she had never asked him about and used without comment.

He opened it. She was holding a sealed container with both hands because it was still hot.

"Extra," she said.

He stepped back — not far, just the half-step that was always there, automatic, old enough that he'd stopped tracking it. She came in and set the container on the counter he kept clear for tools. She pulled her jacket off and put it over the back of the chair he used for equipment runs, which apparently was also now the jacket chair, and neither of them had said anything about that.

The food was real. Not a vend brick, not hydration paste — something she'd made, he could tell from the weight of the container and the smell that came off it when she cracked the seal. Broth. Grain. Something charred at the edges that meant she'd used actual heat. Steam rose between them and went flat.

"Didn't know I needed feeding," Kyle said.

"I had extra."

She was already eating. She had her own portion in a smaller container and was standing at his counter with it, using the near edge of the surface the way she always did — half on the counter, half in her hand, her back to the far wall. He hadn't noticed when that had become her spot.

Kyle looked at the container she'd left him.

He didn't eat. Not yet. He didn't move it either.

She fished a blister strip from her jacket pocket — the jacket on the equipment chair — and pressed out a small white tab. Split it in half with her thumbnail. Set one piece on the counter beside his container without announcing it and took the other one herself.

"Medithadol," she said, though he hadn't asked.

"I know what medithadol looks like."

"Just checking."

She ate. He stood. The steam went flat.

He picked up the container eventually — not the tab, the container — and ate standing beside her. It was good. The grain had absorbed the broth all the way through, which took time. He didn't say so.

"You're running a job."

"Day after tomorrow."

"You're thinking about it tomorrow."

He ate.

"Lotus territory," she said. "Corridor work."

He hadn't told her that. He hadn't not told her either. She had her own clients and her own ways of knowing things, and he had found that pointing out either fact produced a kind of patient silence that felt worse than not pointing it out.

"The draw angle on Cacophony," she said. "You've got the ride too low."

He looked at the revolver on the counter — clipped to the edge, where it lived when he was home.

"You clip your elbow on a tight inside draw. I noticed it last month during calibration. High-quarter pull against a close wall — you'll swing wide before the barrel clears."

"I know how I draw."

"I know you know how you draw." She scraped the last of her broth. "I'm telling you what I saw. Raise the ride height two centimeters, or tilt the whole rig butt-forward five degrees. Corridor walls being what they are."

He looked at the holster. She was right about the clip — he'd felt it once or twice on tight doorframes and written it off as clearance. He didn't say she was right.

"You can fix it before the job," she said. "It's not a thing."

She capped her container and dropped it in his recycler, which was close enough to her own that she apparently regarded them as interchangeable. She put her jacket back on.

Kyle reached over and picked up the half-tab from the counter. Took it.

"Eat the rest," she said, nodding at his container. "The grain gets stiff."

She left. He heard 2E's lock engage across the hall.

The holster sat on the counter where it always sat. He looked at it.

He ate the rest of the grain, which had gotten stiff. It was still good. He put the container in the recycler and didn't touch the holster.

interludes.label: The Pill
interludes.title: The Pill
interludes.synopsis: They take a mild hallucinogen together. Both perceive the same impossible geometry — a fifth wall, a pulse through the floor. Nobody takes credit. Kyle files it as undetermined.
interludes.text:
The Dusk tab split the room at the edges, and the edges didn't fight it.

They were on the floor of 2E — Pixel's back against the workbench housing, his against the south wall, a gap between them of maybe two feet that contracted and expanded depending on what he was paying attention to. She'd put music on and turned it low enough that the rhythm came and went. The light strip was at the warm end of its range. The workbench was folded up and the cables were run along the shelving with the precision that made her apartment feel like a well-maintained instrument.

This was the part that cost nothing. They were good at it.

Pixel was explaining something about a client's array — a modification that had been installed wrong, not wrong enough to refuse payment, wrong enough that she would remember it. She talked with her hands when she was quietly irritated. Her hands were moving.

"He thought he was paying for the premium," she said. "He was paying for the premium. He got standard tolerances in premium housing, and he can't tell the difference, and I have to decide whether to tell him."

"Will you?"

"I haven't decided."

"You already decided."

She looked at him.

"You'd have already told him if you weren't going to," Kyle said.

She was quiet. Then: "The part that irritates me is that he'll be fine."

"Most of them are."

"That's the irritating part."

The music moved. The light strip ran warm. He was watching the room without thinking about it — the kind of looking that the Dusk permitted, easy and unfocused — and at some point he became aware he was counting the walls.

He went around: east wall, north wall with its shelving, west wall, south wall with the folded bench. Four. He went around again, this time slower, tracking where the light sat against each surface. East. North. West.

Between west and south there was a fifth.

Not a wall. Not a shape he could name. A surface, or the suggestion of one — something that existed in the interval between west and south, in a space where the room's actual geometry had no room for an interval. He held still and tried to find it directly. When he looked at the place it should be, the corner was just a corner, west meeting south at ninety degrees, the seam where the paint had been lapped twice.

He stopped looking.

The fifth thing came back.

He went around one more time, slowly. East. North. West. The interval. South. Five. Then he looked and it was four. He sat with that.

"Hey," Pixel said.

He looked at her.

She was watching the same corner. Her hand was on the floor between them, palm down, fingers spread — not reaching, not bridging the gap. Checking.

"Same thing," she said. Not a question.

"Yes."

The music had stopped. He hadn't heard it stop.

Neither of them said what the thing was. Naming it would have required a category, and neither of them had a category for a geometry that was larger on the inside than the count permitted. He knew what Dusk did — the softening, the colors deepening, the way time slowed in the gaps between things. It did not produce additional walls. It did not produce precision. Whatever this was, it was precise.

Then the pulse came up through the floor.

Low. Below hearing. He felt it in the bones of his seat and in his palms where they pressed against the floor — a vibration that ran at some frequency the body registers before the mind does, slow and even. One. Two. Three. Four. Then nothing.

Pixel let out a breath.

The room was four-walled. The corner was a corner. The light strip ran warm. After a while she started talking again — not immediately, not pretending — returning when she was ready, the client and the array and whether she would tell him. He answered when she asked him things. It came back: the ordinary room, the floor, the two feet between them. She laughed once at something she said herself.

He stayed another hour. The foot between them had closed to eight inches at some point and neither of them had noted it.

When he left she walked him to the door. They stood in the hallway between 2E and 2W for a moment — his door was right there, there was no reason to stand in a hallway, they both stood in it anyway.

He crossed over.

Inside 2W in the dark he brought up the array. Everything running. Vitals nominal. The Atlas NeoCortex logged no spike, no surge, no timestamp flagged. Whatever had moved through the room had not moved through his system. Or had moved through it without registering. He held that distinction for a moment, then let it go.

He filed it as undetermined.

He slept.

interludes.label: The Knock
interludes.title: The Knock
interludes.synopsis: Kyle knocks once on the wall. Fifteen minutes later Pixel is at his door, soldering iron in hand. 'You eat?' He follows. The book exhales.
interludes.text:
The apartment had a crack in the east wall, just above the junction box, and at this hour the lumen mice found it. They came in threes and fours, thumbnail-sized, their bodies casting cold blue-green light that traced paths across the ceiling like slow sparks. Kyle had lived in 2W for six years without once disturbing them. Whatever agreement existed between him and the mice, it was the oldest one he had.

He sat on the floor with his back against the couch, in the dark except for them.

He had written two words in a ledger tonight and an eleven-year intelligence had agreed to them. He had a loop closed he hadn't known was open. Nine predecessors he would never meet, and a name at the end of everything: Marrow. The Office's West Town program was burned. Locally was a word he was still examining for exits.

The bike was gone.

He kept returning to this the way a tongue finds a missing tooth — not because it was the worst thing, but because it was the one thing he'd had no policy for. Two days he had carried its absence and it still did not fit anywhere he'd been trained to put things. He had bought it himself. With money earned for work he had chosen, in a year when he had chosen more things than usual. It had no history before him. That was what he had liked about it.

The mice lit a slow arc across the ceiling and went back through the crack.

He sat for a while.

Then he stood and went to the east wall — the shared wall, 2E — and lifted his right hand and knocked once.

Not twice. Not the kind of knock that arrives with its hands out. Just: once. The ferrocement held the sound a half-second and let it go.

He went back to the couch.

The building settled somewhere above him — a thermal tick, nothing more. He did not run a threat matrix. He did not have a job on deck. He sat in his apartment at 0200 and did not reach for anything to do with his hands.

Fifteen minutes. Her door, then his.

She was in the same clothes she'd been in at the trace site. She had the soldering iron in her left hand, indicator amber — still warm — which meant she had been at the workbench when the knock came through and had not set the iron down first, had not changed, had not weighed it. She had just come. A small spool of silver wire had caught on the lead near the grip and she hadn't noticed it.

She looked at him.

"You eat?"

He had not eaten. He considered this for approximately one second.

He stood up and got his jacket from the hook by the door — the other one, not the field jacket. She had already turned back into the corridor.

He followed her out.

The door to 2W closed behind him. He didn't hold it open or check the latch. The hall light was the same amber it had been at this hour for six years.

He followed her.
